Republican Senator Susan Collins says she is not President Trump's favorite senator.
And during a debate Tuesday night against her Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson, Collins
criticized the Iran war.
It is not well thought out.
It has caused adverse circumstances in terms of the cost of global oil.
Collins argued that she has maintained her political independence, saying she's voted
against Trump more than she did when Democrat Joe Biden was president.
But Jackson sought to tie her closely to the Trump administration, saying he will better
represent the people of Maine.
Senator Collins has had 30 years to show whose side she's on.
I don't owe Donald Trump and the billionaires anything.
I don't fight for billionaires like she does.
I owe Mainers everything.
And that's who I'm going to be fighting for when I'm the next U.S. senator.
The debate was the first.
Between the two, they are to engage in three more later this month.
Walt Disney Company argued in court Tuesday that the Trump administration is violating
its First Amendment rights.
The focus is on eight local ABC TV stations owned by Disney.
NPR's David Folk and Flick reports the FCC launched early reviews for those stations'
licenses.
FCC chief Brendan Carr didn't attend the hearing, but he loomed large over it.
President Trump has blasted ABC repeatedly for its content and coverage, and Carr has
echoed him.
Disney's attorney said the very threat that those licenses could be taken away has chilled
ABC's free speech.
Its attorney said ABC News carried a Trump White House address in July on its streaming
service only because it feared retaliation if it didn't.
The U.S. Justice Department's lawyers argued the dispute should be resolved through a bureaucratic
appeal process, not the district court.
And the government said the review of the station's licenses was needed to get more
information about Disney's diversity initiatives.
The judge sounded dubious about that claim.
David Folk and Flick, NPR News.
Now to France, where more than 250,000 students took to the streets of major cities Tuesday
to continue to press their demands for better conditions at school, NPR's owner Beardsley
reports.
Paris's Place de la République was packed with high schoolers who sang the Marseillaise
and chanted revolutionary slogans.
There were also parents and teachers.
All say more needs to be spent on education.
Some kids from well-off neighborhoods are taking part in the movement out of solidarity
for those in the poor suburbs and rural areas where schools are not as tended to.
Critics say the government spent too long ignoring the protests and then treated them
as a security problem.
Protesters say a strong and egalitarian education system is at the heart of France's meritocracy
and democracy.
France has a huge deficit and the government is looking for places to cut, not spend.
There are fears the protests on top of rising energy prices could lead to further social
disruption.
Eleanor Beardsley, NPR News, Paris.
This is NPR.
Convicted killer Christa Pike has regained consciousness and is speaking that word from
her lawyers who said in a statement Tuesday that she is still handcuffed and shackled
to her hospital bed as she receives treatment following last week's failed execution by
the state of Tennessee.
Police say a court hearing is scheduled for Wednesday on their request to preserve evidence.
A former CIA official has pleaded guilty to wire fraud.
NPR's Ryan Lucas reports on the arrest of the man at his home where agents recovered
more than $40 million worth of gold bars.
The defendant, David Rush, was a senior official in the CIA.
He was arrested in May and FBI agents found nearly 300 gold bars, more than $2 million
in cash, as well as luxury watches at his Virginia home.
He was initially charged with theft of public money.
Now, according to his plea agreement, Rush acknowledges he fabricated highly classified
government programs and activities in order to siphon off government funds, including
the gold bars, to enrich himself to the tune of some $194 million.
Court papers say Rush has pleaded guilty to one count of wire fraud.
He faces a maximum sentence of 20 years, plus forfeiture, restitution, and a fine.
His sentencing is scheduled for late January.
Ryan Lucas, NPR News, Washington.
Oscar winner Eva Marie Saint has died.
Saint's family announced that she died Tuesday at her home in Los Angeles.
She was 102 years old.
She won her Academy Award as supporting actress for her first movie on the waterfront and
played a spy in Alfred Hitchcock's North by Northwest opposite Cary Grant.
